title: TLS Handshake and Certificate Chain
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The TLS handshake negotiates cryptographic parameters, authenticates the server through a certificate chain to a trusted root, and derives a shared session key. Subsequent records use authenticated encryption.
short: Negotiate, authenticate, derive keys, then protect traffic.
long: Negotiate, authenticate, derive keys, then protect traffic. Certificate revocation checking and hostname verification are essential parts of authentication in practice.
proof: Signatures chain from a trusted root through intermediates to the server's certificate, and an ephemeral key exchange produces a session key known only to the endpoints.
consequence: TLS is the foundation of confidentiality and integrity on the web.

title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack on Unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Unauthenticated Diffie–Hellman is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack: an attacker creates one shared secret with each party and relays traffic, which neither party can detect.
short: Secret sharing without authentication gives no assurance about who the peer is.
long: Secret sharing without authentication gives no assurance about who the peer is. Digital signatures or certificates on the exchanged public values authenticate the parties and prevent the attack.
proof: Each endpoint accepts the attacker's public value as coming from the other party, so the attacker shares a key with each and can decrypt and re-encrypt relayed messages.
consequence: Authentication is a necessary companion to key agreement.

title: Perfect Forward Secrecy with Ephemeral Keys
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Perfect forward secrecy ensures that compromising a long-term private key does not reveal past session keys. It is achieved by generating fresh ephemeral keys per session and discarding them afterwards.
short: Past sessions stay secret even if today's long-term key leaks.
long: Past sessions stay secret even if today's long-term key leaks. TLS 1.3 requires ephemeral key exchange for this reason; static RSA key transport does not provide forward secrecy.
proof: Each session key depends on ephemeral exponents that are no longer stored, so later knowledge of the long-term signing key cannot reconstruct them.
consequence: Forward secrecy limits the damage of delayed key compromise.

title: Challenge-Response Authentication
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Challenge–response authentication proves knowledge of a secret by requiring a correct reply to a fresh random challenge. Freshness prevents an eavesdropper from replaying a previously recorded response.
short: A new random question makes old answers useless.
long: A new random question makes old answers useless. The function may be a keyed hash, encryption, or digital signature depending on the setting.
proof: A freshly generated challenge makes the probability that a recorded response matches negligible, so a valid reply demonstrates current knowledge of the secret.
consequence: Challenge–response is a core pattern in authentication protocols.

title: Nonces Prevent Replay Attacks
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: A nonce is a value used only once, typically generated freshly at random. Including nonces in authenticated messages lets a receiver detect replayed messages from earlier runs.
short: A fresh one-time value distinguishes this run from every earlier run.
long: A fresh one-time value distinguishes this run from every earlier run. Nonces may be random numbers or counters, but they must not repeat within the relevant security context.
proof: The receiver compares the nonce with values seen in current runs; an old message carries a nonce that does not match a freshly generated one.
consequence: Nonces are a simple and widely used freshness mechanism.

title: Bell-LaPadula Confidentiality Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Bell–LaPadula model enforces confidentiality using two rules: no read up, so a subject cannot read a higher classification, and no write down, so it cannot write to a lower classification.
short: Information may flow upward in sensitivity but never downward.
long: Information may flow upward in sensitivity but never downward. The simple security property and the star property are state invariants of the model, applied to subjects and objects with security levels.
proof: Forbidding reads from higher levels and writes to lower levels prevents information from reaching a subject with insufficient clearance.
consequence: The model is the classical formal basis for mandatory access control.

title: Biba Integrity Model
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The Biba integrity model is the dual of Bell–LaPadula: subjects may not read lower-integrity data and may not write to higher-integrity data, preventing contamination of trusted information.
short: Reverse the information-flow rules to protect integrity rather than secrecy.
long: Reverse the information-flow rules to protect integrity rather than secrecy. Biba uses integrity levels and can be combined with confidentiality models when both properties matter.
proof: Reversing the direction of Bell–LaPadula's flow restrictions keeps low-integrity data from influencing high-integrity objects.
consequence: Biba is the standard formal model for integrity policies.

title: Capability-Based Security
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: In capability-based security, possession of an unforgeable reference called a capability grants authority over an object. A capability combines designation and permission in one transferable token.
short: Holding the unforgeable token is the authority.
long: Holding the unforgeable token is the authority. Capabilities may be implemented with kernel-protected handles or unguessable cryptographic tokens, and they support fine-grained delegation.
proof: Because capabilities cannot be forged or guessed without being granted, only a holder can name and access the object with the encoded rights.
consequence: Capability systems avoid ambient authority and make least privilege easier to enforce.

title: Access Control Lists versus Capabilities
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Access control lists attach a list of permitted principals to each object, whereas capabilities attach permissions to the reference a principal holds. The two are dual in where authority is stored.
short: ACLs ask who may access an object; capabilities ask what the bearer may do.
long: ACLs ask who may access an object; capabilities ask what the bearer may do. Delegation is easy with capabilities but awkward with ACLs, while revocation is often easier with ACLs.
proof: An ACL is consulted at the object on each access, while a capability is presented with the request; passing a capability simply transfers the reference.
consequence: The distinction shapes the design of operating systems and distributed authorization systems.

title: Principle of Least Privilege
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: The principle of least privilege grants each component only the permissions it needs for its legitimate task and no more. It limits damage from accidents and compromised components.
short: Give exactly the permissions required, nothing more.
long: Give exactly the permissions required, nothing more. It applies to users, processes, and services, and is implemented through roles, sandboxing, and scoped tokens.
proof: Restricting rights reduces the set of actions available to a faulty or compromised component, bounding the harm it can cause.
consequence: Least privilege is a baseline requirement in security engineering.

title: Defence in Depth
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Defence in depth layers independent security controls so that failure of one does not expose the system. Typical layers include firewalls, authentication, encryption, logging, and input validation.
short: Several independent barriers are safer than one perfect one.
long: Several independent barriers are safer than one perfect one. The principle acknowledges that individual controls fail and aims to slow or detect an attacker rather than rely on a single boundary.
proof: An attacker must defeat several independent controls, so overall compromise probability is lower than with a single control.
consequence: Layered defences reduce risk from both known and unknown vulnerabilities.

title: Password Salting against Rainbow Tables
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Salting stores a unique random value with each password hash so identical passwords produce different hashes. Precomputed rainbow tables become ineffective because each salt requires its own table.
short: A per-account random value defeats precomputed password tables.
long: A per-account random value defeats precomputed password tables. Salts need not be secret, but they must be unique and generated with sufficient randomness.
proof: Including a different salt per account in the hash input means a precomputed chain for one salt cannot be reused for another account.
consequence: Salting is mandatory in any password storage scheme.

title: Key Stretching with bcrypt
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Key stretching applies a deliberately expensive iterative computation to a password before storing the derived value. Schemes such as bcrypt slow offline guessing while keeping legitimate logins tolerable.
short: Make every password guess expensive.
long: Make every password guess expensive. The work factor can be increased over time as hardware gets faster. Memory-hard schemes such as Argon2 also limit GPU and ASIC advantages.
proof: An attacker must repeat the full work factor for every guess, so raising the iteration count increases attack cost linearly while each legitimate login pays it only once.
consequence: Key stretching substantially raises the cost of offline cracking.

title: Multifactor Authentication Factors
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Multifactor authentication requires credentials from at least two distinct categories: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is. Combining categories reduces the impact of a single stolen credential.
short: Two different kinds of evidence beat two of the same kind.
long: Two different kinds of evidence beat two of the same kind. A password plus a hardware token is stronger than two passwords because the attack surfaces differ.
proof: Compromising one factor leaves at least one independent barrier, so an attacker must break multiple distinct mechanisms.
consequence: Multifactor authentication is recommended for high-value accounts.

title: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework in which a client obtains a limited access token from an authorization server and uses it with a resource server. It delegates access without sharing the resource owner's credentials.
short: Delegate limited access using scoped, expiring tokens.
long: Delegate limited access using scoped, expiring tokens. Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for public clients; implicit flows are deprecated.
proof: The token encodes scope and expiry, so the client acts only within the granted permissions and the resource owner's password never reaches it.
consequence: OAuth 2.0 is the dominant delegation protocol for web APIs.

title: Zero Trust Architecture
subject: Cryptography & Security
statement: Zero trust architecture assumes no implicit trust based on network location and requires continuous verification of identity, device state, and policy for every access request.
short: Network position is not evidence of trustworthiness.
long: Network position is not evidence of trustworthiness. It replaces perimeter-based defences with per-request authentication, authorisation, and least-privilege access.
proof: Treating each request independently means a breached internal host gains no automatic access to other resources, limiting lateral movement.
consequence: Zero trust guides the design of modern enterprise and cloud networks.

title: Linear Temporal Logic Semantics
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Linear temporal logic extends propositional logic with operators over time along a single path: next, eventually, globally, and until. Formulas are evaluated at positions of an infinite execution trace.
short: Express properties of sequences, such as eventually reaching a goal.
long: Express properties of sequences, such as eventually reaching a goal. LTL is interpreted over linear traces, in contrast to branching-time logics such as CTL. Safety and liveness properties are naturally written in LTL.
proof: The semantics are recursive on traces: eventually holds if some future position satisfies p, globally if all positions do, and p until q if q holds at a future point with p holding before it.
consequence: LTL is the standard specification language for model checkers of reactive systems.

title: Computation Tree Logic and Branching Time
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Computation tree logic quantifies over branching futures using path quantifiers A and E combined with temporal operators. It expresses claims such as 'on all paths eventually p' or 'there exists a path where p holds until q'.
short: Branching-time logic asks whether all or some futures satisfy a temporal property.
long: Branching-time logic asks whether all or some futures satisfy a temporal property. CTL differs from LTL by allowing path quantification at every temporal operator, making it suitable for state-based model checking.
proof: A formula is evaluated at a state of a transition system by considering all or some outgoing paths and applying the temporal operator along each chosen path.
consequence: CTL is the specification language of several classical model checkers.

title: Kripke Structures for Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Kripke structure consists of states, a transition relation between them, and a labelling of states with atomic propositions. It is the standard semantic model for temporal-logic model checking.
short: A labelled transition system gives temporal formulas a precise meaning.
long: A labelled transition system gives temporal formulas a precise meaning. Paths through the structure represent possible executions, and total transition relations ensure every finite prefix has an extension.
proof: The transition relation generates all executions and the labelling determines which atomic propositions hold at each state, giving an interpretation of temporal formulas.
consequence: Model-checking algorithms compute the set of states satisfying a formula over such a structure.

title: Safety and Liveness Properties
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Safety properties state that nothing bad ever happens, while liveness properties state that something good eventually happens. Every property of infinite traces is the intersection of a safety property and a liveness property.
short: Safety is refuted by a finite prefix; liveness needs an infinite trace.
long: Safety is refuted by a finite prefix; liveness needs an infinite trace. Mutual exclusion is safety, while eventual progress is liveness. Deadlock freedom combines aspects of both.
proof: Safety violations occur at some finite prefix, whereas liveness violations require an infinite trace with no good event; this distinction yields the decomposition theorem for trace properties.
consequence: The distinction determines what kind of counterexample a model checker must produce.

title: State Explosion Problem in Model Checking
subject: Formal Methods
statement: The global state space of a concurrent system grows roughly as the product of its components' state counts, making explicit enumeration infeasible for large systems.
short: Composing components multiplies their state spaces.
long: Composing components multiplies their state spaces. Symbolic representations, partial-order reduction, symmetry reduction, and abstraction all attack different aspects of the explosion.
proof: A global state is a tuple of component states, so the number of possible tuples is the product of component counts and is exponential in the number of components.
consequence: Coping with state explosion is the central engineering challenge of model checking.

title: Symbolic Model Checking with BDDs
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Symbolic model checking represents sets of states and transition relations with reduced ordered binary decision diagrams rather than enumerating states individually. This can compress exponentially many states into manageable graphs.
short: Represent whole state sets as Boolean functions.
long: Represent whole state sets as Boolean functions. Reachability is computed by repeated image operations on BDDs until a fixed point is reached.
proof: A reduced ordered BDD is a canonical representation of a Boolean function; applying image and preimage operators symbolically computes reachable states without visiting each state one at a time.
consequence: BDD-based checking verified many hardware designs with enormous state spaces.

title: Bounded Model Checking with SAT
subject: Formal Methods
statement: Bounded model checking encodes the existence of a counterexample of length k as a propositional formula. A satisfying assignment gives a concrete execution trace violating the property.
short: Search for a short violating trace using a SAT solver.
long: Search for a short violating trace using a SAT solver. Increasing k gives completeness up to a bound, while induction or diameter bounds can establish absence of longer counterexamples.
proof: The formula encodes the transition relation for k steps and the negation of the property at some step, so any satisfying assignment describes a valid error trace.
consequence: Advances in SAT solving have made BMC highly effective for hardware and software.

title: Bisimulation Equivalence
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A bisimulation is a relation between states of two transition systems such that related states match each other's moves and reach related successors. Bisimilar states satisfy the same branching-time temporal formulas.
latex: R\subseteq S_1\times S_2,\quad s_1\ R\ s_2
short: Two systems are equivalent if each can mimic the other's every move.
long: Two systems are equivalent if each can mimic the other's every move. Bisimulation is finer than trace equivalence because it preserves branching structure, not merely the set of observable sequences.
proof: The back-and-forth conditions let every step from one state be matched from the related state, so modal and branching-time formulas cannot distinguish them.
consequence: Bisimulation is the standard behavioural equivalence for concurrent processes.

title: Petri Nets Model Concurrent Systems
subject: Formal Methods
statement: A Petri net is a bipartite graph of places and transitions in which tokens mark places and enabled transitions consume tokens from inputs and produce tokens on outputs. It models concurrency, synchronisation, and resource sharing.
short: Token flows describe concurrent activity and resource use.
long: Token flows describe concurrent activity and resource use. Place invariants and transition invariants support static analysis of reachability and boundedness properties.
proof: A transition fires only when its input places hold enough tokens, and the marking update records the resulting distribution, so firing sequences represent concurrent executions.
consequence: Petri nets are widely used to model protocols, workflows, and manufacturing systems.
